title: Reserve governor: IGR a ‘call to action’
full_text:
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has labelled Treasury’s Intergenerational Report a “call to action” for governments and business to address the nation’s dire productivity levels, while questioning how useful the artificial intelligence boom will be in lifting it.
AI was a key factor underpinning the Albanese government’s productivity assumption of a 1.2 per cent average annual growth rate for the next 40 years, which some economists have said was overly optimistic even if the best AI outcomes were included.
“Artificial intelligence is developing rapidly, and will be a defining influence on the economy over the next 40 years,” the IGR said. “AI will likely boost productivity by improving efficiency and unlocking new innovations, but there are a wide range of potential future outcomes.” The RBA governor on Tuesday said she didn’t want to get into a debate about whether the report’s productivity assumption was fair enough or not, but weighed in on government’s role and whether there was an AI bubble.
“Some people think it’s a bubble, some people don’t. I don’t have a particular view one way or the other, but it’s a risk that I think we’re watching,” Ms Bullock told a lunch hosted by the Committee for Economic Development of Australia in Sydney on Tuesday.
“It might not be a bubble, but it might be. And if it unwinds in a disorderly manner, then that could have implications for the financial system and also for the real economies.” Amid an estimated $180bn in AI investment expected in Australia from companies such as Nvidia, Anthropic, OpenAI, Amazon, Google and Microsoft, Ms Bullock said earlier in her fireside chat that there was little evidence AI was actively boosting the economy’s productive capacity, but was contributing to excess demand in the Australian economy.
“We’ve got this sort of awkward sequencing event at the moment where, in Australia at least, we are in a situation of excess demand and the AI boom is adding to that demand ahead of any potential supply impacts that it might have going forward,” she said.
She said the Intergenerational Report’s assumptions about productivity – which included lower- and higher-case scenarios of 0.8 per cent and 1.6 per cent productivity – were key to the future of the Australian economy.
“I think the start point that many have made is that the productivity assumption is obviously something that’s really key to the outcomes here,” Ms Bullock said.
“I don’t want to buy into discussions about whether or not it’s too optimistic or not.
“One way to look at that is to say, ‘Well, this is our call to action to get productivity done. This is the call to action’, and that’s the way I would like to think about it.” The RBA, which looks set to make its fourth interest rate hike this year, suggested government could also help by lifting productivity through stimulating business investment.
“People often turn to the government for that, and look, there are things governments can do. They can remove red tape. They can make it easier for businesses to invest. They can make it rewarding for businesses to innovate,” Ms Bullock said. “Things governments could be doing is how do they encourage competition as well, so that will also help to possibly spur productivity.
“So they’re the sorts of things that governments can do. But businesses also have to step up to the plate as well.” Ms Bullock also noted Labor’s changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing were also having an impact. “You can see very directly the impact of the tax changes, because you can see housing approvals for investors have just dropped,” she said.
